newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank wages conflicts hots up before talks.
newsitem.headline: German bank wages conflicts hots up before talks.

text.p: Fresh conflicts emerged on Monday in the dispute between German bank staff and employers over hotly-contested reductions in sick pay allowances, raising the risk of more worker protests before Christmas.

A week before official wage round talks for the sector are due to start, Horst Mueller, chief negotiator for the bank employers, told a news conference that banks would not respond to demands to drop the controversial sick pay cuts.
"We regard the 20 percent cut in sick pay as unavoidable," Mueller said, adding that bank personnel costs had reached an unacceptable level.

German banks last month implemented a new law allowing employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent of normal pay from the 100 percent which applied before, triggering protests on a scale not normally seen in the peaceable banking sector.

The DAG white collar workers' union reacted angrily to Mueller's remarks, accusing him of "pouring oil on the fire of the wage dispute" by setting preconditions in advance of the official wage talks, which are due to start next Monday.

DAH chief negotiator Gerhard Renner said in a statement: "If employers insist on punishing ill employees by cutting their pay at the December 9 talks, they will have to expect union reaction coming up to Christmas."
More than 15,000 German bank staff took to the streets in November in protest at the sick pay cuts -- in a highly unusual demonstration of bank employee defiance.
Similar attempts to cut sick pay in the metals and engineering sectors triggered widespread walk-outs and forced employers to defer the reductions.

But Mueller said the cuts in sick pay would shave only 0.5 to one percent off total wage costs for banks, and said supplementary wage costs in the sector were now as high as the total cost of regular salaries.
Banks would also be seeking to establish more flexible working hours at next week's talks in order to allow them to open branches longer on weekdays and on Saturdays, he said.
